question: Between 2005 and 2020, the number of farms in the EU decreased by 37 %, while in Greece more than 300 000 farms were lost. In 2024, the EU cattle population decreased by 2.8 %, sheep by 1.7 % and goats by 1.6 %, with Greece particularly affected by zoonotic diseases – such as pox, which resulted in the killing of 185 110 sheep and goats in in 2024 and 2025.

This decline is increasing dependency on imports, undermining food sovereignty and increasing the environmental footprint. The policies of the European Green Deal and the farm to fork strategy are exacerbating the problem, due to high production costs and bureaucratic hurdles for small farms. In view of the above, can the Commission say: 1.
What specific measures will it take to address the decline in livestock populations in Greece and to strengthen extensive livestock farming, especially in view of the new CAP post-2027?

Will it review the policies of the Green Deal to strike a balance between environmental criteria and economic sustainability for small farmers, reducing red tape and improving compensation for zoonotic diseases?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.2.2026) The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plan 2023-2027 (CSP) for Greece1 supports livestock production notably via coupled support but also for environmental management of livestock systems, animal welfare, reducing the use of antibiotics in sheep and goat farming, investments in biosecurity and in restoring the agricultural potential.

The Commission’s new CAP post-2027 proposal2 offers Member States significant flexibility to design targeted income support that meets the specific needs of their farmers and territories. The CAP proposal makes risk management schemes more flexible and reinforces the crisis intervention covering animal diseases.

The Vision for Agriculture and Food recognizes the environmental benefits of extensive livestock systems and calls for ways to support them. The Commission’s new CAP post-2027 proposal aims at rendering more targeted environmental obligations, and at allowing to enhance support for the livestock sector’s competitiveness and sustainability.

The proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council establishing a European Fund for economic, social and territorial cohesion, agriculture and rural, fisheries and maritime, prosperity and security3 increases maximum spending for coupled income support from 13% to 20%, with an additional 5% possible for sectors and regions that need it most.

Payment would be possible for grass production in addition to protein crops that help livestock farms. Farming in areas with-specific constraints would also be supported. Already in 2026 the recently agreed simplification4 in the second CAP package reduces administrative burden of at least EUR 1,6 bn per year for farmers5.
